directAnswer: St. Sylvester I was pope from 314 to 335, the long reign that coincided with Constantine's patronage of the Church. Under him the first great Roman basilicas were built, including St. John Lateran and the original St. Peter's, and the Council of Nicaea met in 325 with his legates present. Later legends made him the baptizer of Constantine and the recipient of the forged Donation of Constantine; neither claim is historical.

sections.h2: Bishop of Rome in Constantine's Empire
paras: Sylvester, a Roman, succeeded Miltiades in January 314 and led the Roman church for almost twenty-two years. That was the period when Christianity moved from a tolerated minority to a faith enjoying imperial favor, and Rome's Christian landscape changed dramatically.

Surprisingly, few of his own writings or decisions survive. The emperor, not the pope, dominated the great ecclesiastical events of the day, and Sylvester appears in the record mostly through his representatives and the churches built during his time.

sections.h2: Arles, Nicaea, and the Papal Legates
paras: Months into his reign, a council at Arles in Gaul met to reconsider the Donatist controversy. Sylvester did not attend but sent two priests and two deacons, and the bishops sent him a letter reporting their decisions.

In 325, Constantine convened the first ecumenical council at Nicaea in Asia Minor to answer the teaching of Arius, who denied that the Son is fully divine. Sylvester, elderly and far away, was represented by two Roman priests, Vitus and Vincentius. The council produced the Nicene Creed, professing the Son to be of one substance with the Father, and settled the method for dating Easter.

Imperial generosity transformed Rome during these years. The Lateran Basilica, today the cathedral of the bishop of Rome, rose beside the former Lateran palace. Over the tomb of St. Peter on the Vatican Hill, construction began on the great basilica that stood until it was replaced in the sixteenth century. A church inside an imperial residence, later known as Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, was associated with relics of the Cross.
The Liber Pontificalis also credits Sylvester with founding a parish church on land given by a priest named Equitius, a foundation connected with the later church of San Martino ai Monti.

sections.h2: Legends: The Baptism of Constantine and the Donation
paras: A fifth-century tale, the Acts of Sylvester, claims that he cured Constantine of leprosy and baptized him in Rome. In fact, Constantine was baptized near the end of his life in 337, near Nicomedia, by Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia.

That legend fed the Donation of Constantine, a document most likely forged in the eighth century, in which the emperor supposedly granted Sylvester and his successors authority over Rome and the western provinces. It was cited for centuries in disputes over papal power until fifteenth-century scholars, notably Lorenzo Valla, demonstrated that it could not be authentic.

Sylvester died on December 31, 335, and was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla. His feast falls on the last day of the year, which is why New Year's Eve is called Silvester in much of Europe; Eastern Christians honor him on January 2.

keyFacts: Pope from 314 to 335, during the reign of Constantine
Sent legates to the Council of Arles (314) and the Council of Nicaea (325)
His reign saw the building of the Lateran Basilica and Old St. Peter's
The Donation of Constantine attributed to him is a medieval forgery
Feast day December 31 in the West, January 2 in the East

faqs.question: Did Pope Sylvester I baptize Constantine?
faqs.answer: No. That story comes from a later legend. Historical sources show Constantine was baptized shortly before his death in 337 by Eusebius of Nicomedia.

faqs.question: Did Pope Sylvester attend the Council of Nicaea?
faqs.answer: He did not travel to Nicaea. He was represented by two Roman priests, Vitus and Vincentius, who took part in the council on his behalf.

faqs.question: Why is New Year's Eve called Silvester in some countries?
faqs.answer: Sylvester died on December 31, 335, and his feast is celebrated that day. In Germany, Austria, Poland, and elsewhere, the last night of the year is still named after him.
